title: What Happens When an AI Assistant Answers Every Call You Miss
dek: I replaced my own voicemail with an AI assistant, then turned it into a 24/7 call screener. Here's what it does and why it's worth it for a busy owner.
videoTitle: I Replaced My Voicemail With an AI Agent (Retell AI Tutorial)

body.text: I replaced my voicemail with an AI agent, and it's the one running on my phone right now. When I hit decline, don't answer, or my phone's off, the call goes to Amy, my AI executive assistant, instead of a beep nobody wants to leave a message after.
What a caller hears

In my demo, a guy named Tom calls and asks if I'm around. Amy tells him no, I'm afraid not, he's pretending to be very important right now. Tom asks how much a voice agent costs. Amy explains it depends on the integrations and call volume, and that every agent is scoped and priced case by case. Then she offers to take a message so I can send him a quote.
She asks, "Can I use the number you're calling from?" instead of making him read out ten digits. Small thing, but it makes the call feel a lot smoother.

Her whole job is simple. Screen out spam and politely end those calls. Answer basic questions about my business. And for everyone else, take a message: name, callback number, and the reason for the call.
What I get after the call
A few seconds after Tom hung up, an email landed in my inbox. Who called, why, their number, a summary, and the transcript, plus a button to call them right back. Everything's automated.
It's a safety net. If I hit decline, don't answer, or my phone's off, I always know every single call got handled.

It also didn't take much. Retell's builder drafted the first version of the agent in under 5 minutes from my description, the phone number costs $2 a month, and pointing my real line at it was a forwarding code from my carrier typed into my phone. One gotcha if you're on iPhone: turn off Live Voicemail, because it seems to interfere.
From safety net to 24/7 screener

Here's where it gets more interesting. If the AI can already handle the calls I miss, why only use it when I miss them? The second version answers every call first and only brings me in when I'm actually needed. Perfect if you're getting buried in spam calls and don't want your day interrupted.
I told it exactly who gets through: anyone calling about Oceanside AI Solutions or a voice agent, and my wife. Hopefully nobody pretends to be my wife.

Everyone else gets a few qualifying questions, like where they heard about me. "We met at a conference" is a lot better than "I saw him on YouTube and got his number." The agent uses some judgment there.
When someone qualifies, it does a warm transfer. It rings me first with a quick heads up, like "I've got your wife on the line" or "I've got a hot prospect on the line," and then connects us.
It remembers who called

I also turned on caller memory, so if Bob calls three times, the agent remembers Bob. When I tested it, I called in saying I'd been promised a free voice agent, hung up, then called back and asked if she remembered why I called last time. She did, and picked right back up where we left off. That's what a real assistant would do.

Since it now answers every call, I changed the emails too. I only get one when it matters: a transfer that fails because I didn't pick up, or a conversation the agent judges as high value. No emails for spam, sales pitches, or tire kickers wasting my agent's time.
Pick the level that fits you

We started with something incredibly simple, replacing voicemail, and turned that same agent into a 24/7 screener with transfers, caller memory, and post call summaries. You can stop at whichever level actually makes sense for you.
The point is you don't need some massive complicated system to make your phone life dramatically easier. And if you want something like this built for your business, that's exactly what we do.

title: Can Your AI Agent Legally Call That Number? TCPA Basics
dek: Who you can call, what real consent looks like, and what your agent has to do on every call before you launch an outbound campaign.
videoTitle: AI Cold Calling Laws Explained (TCPA Basics)

body.text: I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice. It's the base I've learned for running outbound campaigns without getting into stupid trouble.

If you're a business owner thinking about having a voice agent make outbound calls, this is what you need to understand first. These laws aren't theory. In February 2026, Mortgage One Funding got hit with two class action lawsuits in 15 days. They ran AI cold calls about refinancing, with no consent, to numbers on the Do Not Call list.
Your AI agent counts as a robocall

In February 2024 the FCC unanimously ruled that an AI generated voice is an artificial voice under the TCPA. That means your agent is regulated exactly like a prerecorded message, under rules that go back to 1991. Doesn't matter how conversational it sounds.

A big reason why: right before the New Hampshire primary in January 2024, about 5,000 voters got a call from a Joe Biden voice clone telling them to stay home. The FCC proposed a $6 million fine against the organizer, and the carrier that let the traffic through paid $1 million.

Fines are per call. Not per campaign, not per complaint. Per call. That's $500 each, and up to $1,500 if a court decides you did it willfully or knowingly. 100 bad calls at $500 is $50,000. ViSalus made about 1.8 million illegal calls and got hit with $925 million. Dish Network made 51,000 and got $61 million.
Who you can call: consumer or business
Every outbound list goes through one question first. Whose number is this? A consumer's personal phone, or a business line?

If it's a consumer and the call is marketing, meaning you're selling something, offering a promotion, or setting a sales appointment, you need prior express written consent. That's a signed agreement naming your company and that phone number.

If it's a consumer and the call is purely informational, like an appointment reminder with no upsell, the bar is lower. Prior express consent is enough. But watch it. If the agent drifts into "by the way, we're running a discount on such and such," that reminder just became a marketing call and the written consent rules apply.

Business to business is way simpler than people think. All the noise about AI agents needing written consent to call out is about consumers. Calling a verified business landline without written consent is fine, even for a marketing call. The catch: plenty of contractors, spas, HVAC and roofing companies use a personal cell as the business number. Cross those off, because you're right back in consumer territory.
What real consent looks like

A checkbox alone doesn't cut it. The language matters. Mine reads along these lines: I agree that Oceanside AI Solutions may contact me at the number provided using an automatic dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice, and text messages, for marketing purposes. I understand consent is not required and that I can opt out at any time by replying STOP.
If it doesn't mention an artificial or prerecorded voice, it does NOT cover your AI agent. And texting permission through A2P is not the same as permission for AI voice calls. Two different things.

You also need proof. The person suing never has to prove they didn't consent. You have to prove they did. So keep the timestamp, the checkbox, their phone number, and the exact disclosure text. The IP address isn't technically required right now, but I'd collect it anyway.

Old leads come up a lot. A business wants to point an agent at a pile of old leads to bring them back. If those leads never gave proper written consent, you can't just call them to ask for it. Email them, explain clearly what you're asking, send them to a landing page with an unchecked opt in box, and only call the people who opt in. Painful, but that's how it works.
What your agent has to do on every call

Three things on every artificial voice call. Identify who's calling. Give a callback number. And keep an internal do not call list, so when someone says stop, the agent records it somewhere you can check later, even a Google Sheet.

Does it have to announce it's an AI up front? At the federal level, no. California's AB 2905, effective January 1, 2025, does require the agent to say it's an AI at the very start of the call. My rule of thumb everywhere: if someone asks, the agent answers honestly. Yes, I'm an AI.

States also stack their own rules on top of the federal ones. Colorado, for example, has its own do not call registry separate from the national list. Check every state you plan to call before launch. I go through a preflight checklist on all of this before any campaign, and I'd want anyone running calls for your business to do the same.

title: Sierra or Retell AI: What I'd Check Before Buying a Voice Agent Platform
dek: I called a live Sierra voice agent and a Retell equivalent back to back. Here's how they compare on speed, ownership, data control, and price.
videoTitle: Sierra vs Retell AI: Which One Should Enterprises Actually Buy?

body.text: Here's where I'm coming from. Sierra markets itself as a premium, white glove enterprise solution. On chat and omnichannel, I think that reputation is absolutely earned. On voice specifically, I don't think the product matches the premium. Rather than just tell you that, I tested it. And for full transparency, Retell is the platform I build my clients' agents on.
The call test

I called Sonos, which runs a real Sierra voice agent, and told it my speaker stopped working. It understood me fine. It asked which model I had, then whether the speaker was shaped more like a cylinder or a rectangle. But the pauses were so long I had to hang up. The intelligence is there, but man.

Then I called a Retell equivalent with the same problem. It asked which product, offered Move or Roam, asked what the glitch was, and started walking me through checking the volume. Quick back and forth, the way a person would do it.
That's not a comprehensive test by any means. But at face value you can already hear clear differences.
Speed is the whole game on the phone

Two humans talking on the phone run around 500 milliseconds between turns. Retell advertises around 620. In reality it's a little higher, but in the best conditions that's what you get. Sierra came in around 1,400 milliseconds at baseline in our own tests, and on that live Sonos call it was a lot worse than that.
I'm not saying Sierra is bad. I'm saying Retell is abnormally good on latency. On an independent voice AI benchmark plotting platforms by performance and latency, Retell came out on top.
If your customers reach you by phone, this isn't a technical detail. Every pause is something the caller sits through.
Who owns the agent when it's done
Both companies will build the agent for you. What happens afterward is not the same.

Retell has forward deployed engineers who'll build the whole thing white glove, like they've done for Lenovo and Motorola. Then, if you want, they transfer full ownership to your own development team to maintain. And because it's an open platform, you can keep customizing it to your exact use case.

Sierra, from what I can tell, is white glove only. The agent lives permanently on their closed platform and they retain 100% ownership. That's vendor lock in, and it's worth knowing before you sign anything.
Who controls your data

Both are SOC 2 certified and both cover HIPAA. The difference is who holds the keys. Sierra runs a managed vault. They hold the audio, the guardrails, and the compliance. In one sense that's peace of mind because they take care of it. In another, it's less control.

Retell works more like a programmable pipe, and it's one of my favorite things about it. There's literally a button to redact personal info like Social Security numbers, credit cards, and passport numbers. If you're under PCI or HIPAA and you have a security team with opinions, controlling the pipe yourself is worth a lot. If you don't have that team, Sierra's managed vault might honestly be the better fit.
Price, and when each one makes sense

Retell posts pay as you go pricing, roughly 7 to 20 cents a minute depending on the model and setup. You can price it out with their calculator today. Sierra reportedly charges per resolution, around $1 to $2.50, and reports I've read put year one at $200k to $350k or more just to get a simple solution built. To find out for sure, you have to get on a sales call.
Sierra has a big name behind it in Bret Taylor, who sits on the board of OpenAI. That doesn't automatically mean a better product.

That said, there is a real space for Sierra. If your support mostly lives in a chat window and you want chat, email, and voice under one contract, the way a lot of ecommerce and software companies do, Sierra might actually be the better choice.

But if the phone IS the business, like healthcare reception, patient intake, or high call volume your team can't absorb, where a pause actually costs you, Retell has clear advantages I don't think Sierra can match. Especially at that price tag.

title: When Your Voice Agent Doesn't Know, It Should Ask You
dek: Human in the loop lets an AI receptionist text or call your manager during the call and relay the answer, so callers stop hearing "we'll get back to you."
videoTitle: Your Voice Agent Needs Human in the Loop (Poku Labs + Retell AI)

body.text: Somebody calls and asks something only a human knows right now. "Do you have this part in stock?" "Can you seat 100 people tonight?" Most voice agents say "we'll get back to you," because they don't have real time info and can't handle the edge cases. In that moment the agent is useless. Sorry, I had to say it.
What if it said "sure, let me text my manager for you, hold on a sec" instead? That's human in the loop, and it's one of the most useful things you can add to a voice agent.
What it sounds like on a real call

In my demo, the agent answers the phone for an auto repair shop. A caller asks for an update on their vehicle. The agent asks to put them on a brief hold, texts the manager on WhatsApp, the manager replies, and the agent comes back with: I've checked with our team and your vehicle will be ready tomorrow.
The caller never sees the text thread behind it. They just get a real answer on the first call.

I built this with Poku Labs connected to Retell AI. Behind the scenes it's a small tool hookup plus instructions telling the agent when to reach out, like whenever someone asks about repair progress or when their vehicle will be ready. Those triggers get tuned to your business. Poku even has a free tier of 20 interactions a month, so it's cheap to try.
A text for routine questions, a phone call for urgent ones

You're not limited to one person or one channel. Sales questions can go to one number, accounting to another, emergencies to a third. You could have five different people each getting the questions meant for them.

For urgent stuff, the agent can call the human instead of texting. People tend to respond faster to a phone call. In my demo a caller says they need a tow right now. The agent calls the owner and explains a customer has an emergency and needs towing. The owner says to tell them he'll call in 10 minutes. The agent hangs up with the owner and relays that straight back to the caller.
What if nobody answers?

You set a time limit, say 60 seconds. If the manager doesn't respond in time, the agent tells the caller the manager isn't available right now and someone will get back to them. So the worst case is the same answer you'd get without it.

Poku also released a newer feature that keeps the conversation open much longer. If the manager answers an hour later, long after the caller hung up, the caller can still get a text from the agent with the manager's answer.
It works for almost any business

This isn't just for auto shops. Real estate, legal, financial services, property management, Airbnb, plumbing, roofing, education, travel and hospitality. Even if you don't deal with time sensitive questions like what's in stock, it works as a safety net. Whenever the agent gets asked something outside its knowledge, it has a way to get the real answer instead of guessing.

My favorite use case: getting email addresses right. Anyone who has tried having a caller spell an email out loud to an AI knows how messy that gets. With this, the agent asks if they'd rather text it. The caller texts it in, and the agent reads back exactly what came through. 100% accurate.

If the thing holding you back from a voice agent is all the questions only you or your manager can answer, this is how I'd handle it. The agent doesn't have to know everything. It has to know who to ask.

title: The Web Form Attack That Can Run Up Your Voice Agent Bill Overnight
dek: Bots hit my demo agent and ran up $137 before I caught it. Someone I know of lost $18,000. Here's how it works and what I do about it now.
videoTitle: My AI Got Attacked… Don't Make This $18,000 Mistake

body.text: My AI got attacked. By the time I caught it, the bill was over $137, and the only reason it was that low is I caught it literally as it started. Others in my community weren't so lucky. One person lost $18,000.

If you have a voice agent that calls people back after they fill out a form on your website, or you're thinking about getting one, you need to know about this. I have a bachelor's degree in cybersecurity, so I look at this as both a builder and someone trained to spot vulnerabilities.
How the attack works
From what I can tell, these attacks target outbound agents, specifically the kind that call someone as soon as they fill out a form on your site. That's exactly the setup I had.

Bots fill out the form over and over with random names and fake company emails. The one thing in common was the phone numbers: rotating UK numbers. And those numbers aren't connected to a person. They're connected to a recording that sounds just human enough to keep your agent talking. "Hi, I have a question." "I can't hear you, I have a sound problem, wait a minute." One kept asking my agent if it spoke Arabic. Meanwhile the meter keeps running.

My best guess on their setup is a basic script spamming forms, cheap internet phone numbers bought in bulk for around a dollar each, and recordings played on repeat. It probably costs them 25 to 100 bucks max. It can cost you thousands overnight.
What it actually cost people

I was literally in a meeting talking about this exact attack. An hour later I pulled up my demo agent to show a friend, something I normally only check about once a week, and my concurrency was maxed out. 20 out of 20 calls happening at the same time. That's not normal. I detached the agent from the number right there.
It was climbing about $10 a minute. If I hadn't caught it, that's $600 by the end of the hour and around $5,000 by the next morning.

One builder in my community lost $450. Another lost $600. Someone he knows got charged $18,000. A friend of mine lost over $300, and the scary part is he had CAPTCHAs and spam filters in place. The bots got around them anyway.
Why do they do it? Honestly, I don't know. I don't see any profit in it for them. My best guess is trolling or harassment. Either way, it's crazy expensive for whoever owns the agent.
Old defenses aren't enough

My friend's story is the lesson. CAPTCHAs and honeypots are the security of yesterday. A honeypot might slow an attacker down like wading through mud, but it's not going to stop them from getting over the wall anymore. We can't expect yesterday's cybersecurity to stop today's AI attacks.
The three protections I use now

First, only call US numbers. The numbers on the platform I build on can now call internationally, and every one of these attacks came from international numbers. That doesn't mean it can't happen with US numbers, but it closes the door they've been walking through.

Second, and this is the big one, a confirmation text. When someone fills out the form and asks for a call, the agent texts them first: hey, this is Mark's agent, just confirming, reply yes if you still want this call. A bot spamming a form can't confirm that text. I don't see a way around it, though I could be wrong.
Third, a cooldown. Make the system wait 60 seconds between calls, or cap it at a couple of calls per minute. Even if something slips through, it can't max out 20 lines at once.
What this means if you own the agent

Don't wait for the bill. If a voice agent is wired to a form on your website right now without protections like these, seriously consider taking it down until they're in. Don't wait until you wake up to a bill of $5,000 or more.
And whoever builds your agent should be able to tell you exactly what stops a bot from making it dial a pile of fake numbers overnight. That's a fair question to ask before anything goes live.

title: Inside the $1,800 Missed Call Agent I Built for a Truck Repair Shop
dek: What the receptionist I built for Big Sky Truck and Trailer Repair actually does, and the decisions that made it worth paying for.
videoTitle: How I Built an $1,800 AI Voice Agent for a Truck Repair Shop

body.text: I sold a voice agent to a real truck repair shop for $1,800. Its job is simple to describe: pick up the calls the team can't get to, answer the basic questions, pull out the details that matter, and email them to the front desk. Here's what went into it, and what I'd want any shop owner to know before buying one.
The job: catch the calls nobody can pick up

The agent is the receptionist for Big Sky Truck and Trailer Repair whenever the team is busy or the shop is closed. That's it. It's not trying to replace the front desk. It covers the calls that would otherwise ring out, including the middle of the night when nobody is there to man the phones.

Every caller goes down one of three paths. A new service request. A status check on a truck that's already in the shop. Or a general question that needs a service advisor to follow up. Each path gets its own instructions, because a driver asking "is my truck done yet" needs a totally different conversation than someone booking a brake job.

On a new service call, the agent gets the caller's name, the make and model, what the truck needs, the best callback number, whether it's drivable or needs a tow, and when they want to drop it off. Then it gives the shop hours and wraps up.
What the shop gets after every call

This is the part owners care about most. When the call ends, the important details get pulled out of the transcript automatically and sent two places. A new row lands in a Google Sheet the managing director can scan. And a clean email hits the front desk: you missed a call from a potential customer, here are the details. Name, number, call type, vehicle, drivable or not, drop off time, a summary, and the recording.
Nobody has to listen to a whole call to figure out who called and when they want to come in. That would be super inefficient.

One small detail I'm proud of. The agent asks if the number they're calling from is the best one to reach them. If the caller says "actually, my wife's number is better," that's the number that shows up in the email. Otherwise it uses the number they called from. Small thing, but it's the difference between a lead you can call back and one you can't.
Built for truckers, not a demo room

A lot of the decisions came from who's calling. Truck drivers call from the road with a ton of background noise. So I turned noise filtering up to aggressive, and I gave the agent permission to say "sorry, I can't hear you, can you speak up?" instead of guessing. Without that, it'll try to answer anyway and probably get it wrong.

Speed mattered too. I chose a slightly less smart model because it's faster. The smarter one pushed response time to almost 1,300 milliseconds versus about 1,000 for the one I picked, and a normal phone call with a friend runs around 500 to 600. When you're talking to truckers, I'll trade a little intelligence for a lot less waiting.

I also kept it lean with no knowledge base. In my experience they add around 50 milliseconds, and the agent gets worse at finding the right answer than if the info just lives in its main instructions.
Guardrails that protect the shop

The agent only answers what it's been told. If the info isn't in its instructions, it says it doesn't have it and writes the question down for a service advisor. That one rule is the biggest thing I've found for keeping an agent from making stuff up.

Pricing gets the same treatment. Ask "how much for a brake job?" and it explains the shop wants to look at the truck first to give an accurate estimate, then asks if you can bring it by. Same answer every time.

It tells the truth if someone asks whether they're talking to an AI. And if a salesperson calls and keeps pitching, two or more times, it politely ends the call instead of burning minutes and wasting the owner's time.
Testing was 40% of the build

About 40% of the two week build went into testing. I ran simulated callers against the agent, like "Bob" calling to check on his truck, and graded each run on whether it followed its steps. Then I tested the whole pipeline from call to inbox, because a great conversation means nothing if the email never reaches the front desk.

That's what I'd push any business owner to ask about. Not just "does it sound human," but "how did you test it, and what happens after the call ends?" And none of this is specific to trucks. Catching missed calls, a few clear paths, and a clean handoff to your team works for pretty much any business that lives on the phone.

title: Retell AI vs ElevenLabs: Which One Should Run Your Business Phone Agent?
dek: I built agents on both platforms and compared realism, testing, telephony, latency, and cost. Here's where each one wins and which one we build client agents on.
videoTitle: Retell AI vs ElevenLabs: The Honest Winner

body.text: If you're shopping for a voice agent, two platform names keep coming up: Retell AI and ElevenLabs. Your agent is going to live on one of them, so it's worth knowing how they actually differ. I've built on both and compared them on pretty much everything, from voice realism to what you'll pay per minute. For full transparency, Retell is what our team builds client agents on. Here's why, and where ElevenLabs honestly beats it.
Where ElevenLabs wins

Realism. I called an ElevenLabs agent I'd just spun up and it was a little scary realistic, not going to lie. Southern accent, cleared its throat, even sneezed and said "excuse me" because I told it to. ElevenLabs gives you surgical precision over exactly how the agent says each word.

Retell can run the same ElevenLabs V3 voice model, and it's not bad. But you don't get that same level of control, so on raw realism ElevenLabs is the clear winner. Same on voices and languages: over 10,000 voices and 70 plus languages, versus Retell's 50 plus languages. ElevenLabs also lets you add languages one by one. On Retell you pick one language or all of them, and turning on all of them raises the chance the agent misreads what a caller said.

Transcription is another ElevenLabs win. Their Scribe V2 model hit a 1.6% word error rate, while Deepgram Nova 3, which I believe is what Retell runs or something very similar, sits around 18% on the same style of test. ElevenLabs also has WhatsApp for voice and text, which matters if your customers are outside the US, plus more plug and play integrations and a faster setup for simple agents.
Where Retell pulls away: testing
For a business, testing is the make or break. It's not enough for an agent to give the right answer once. It has to give it consistently, or that good answer could just be a fluke.

Retell lets us regenerate any single answer 10 times and see how often the agent says what we want. If one of those 10 is wrong, we find it, fix the prompt, and test until it's gone. ElevenLabs' test suite gives you a one time answer, which I can't trust for exactly that reason. On testing, I'd rank ElevenLabs a severe boo.
Retell also has an AI quality assurance suite that can analyze thousands of calls and show what went wrong, with alerts built in. That matters once your agent is handling real callers at volume.
Built for the phone

Retell was designed phone first. ElevenLabs was designed as a voice model with telephony added later. Both connect to Twilio and support SIP trunking, but Retell has the call center features a business actually leans on: warm transfers, keypad (DTMF) handling, and call analytics built in. You can even buy a number right inside the Retell dashboard, which you can't do on ElevenLabs. Convenience matters.

On raw latency ElevenLabs is faster, around 530 milliseconds versus about 600 to 620 on Retell. But on the VAQI benchmark, ElevenLabs flagged significantly more interruptions and misses. So it may respond quicker, but it's more likely to talk over your caller or miss what they said. Retell is a touch slower and makes the caller feel heard, with fewer mistakes on average.
What it costs, and what happens on a busy day

Pricing is basically a tie. On the surface Retell is about 7 cents a minute and ElevenLabs about 8. Once you add the LLM and everything else, my Retell calls average 15 to 20 cents a minute, which is about where ElevenLabs lands too. One caveat: running the ElevenLabs V3 voice on Retell pushes it to around 35 cents a minute all in. ElevenLabs sells subscription tiers, while Retell charges on usage, so you only pay for what you use. I like that a lot better.

Then there's concurrency, meaning how many calls can happen at once. Retell gives you 20 free, then $8 a month per extra slot. It also has a burst option: up to 3x your normal limit, max 300 additional calls, at 10 cents a minute. So if a seasonal rush or an emergency suddenly slams your phones, you're covered without paying every month for capacity you rarely use. On ElevenLabs it's tied to your plan, 4 to 20 on the starter plans, and burst is 2x at around 16 cents a minute.
So which one?

It really depends on your use case. I'd use ElevenLabs for lightweight conversational agents where voice quality is the main requirement, like an ultra realistic voice clone or a simple agent. I'd use Retell for phone operations that are mission critical and running at scale, where accuracy and reliability matter more than the last bit of realism. That's the kind of agent businesses actually pay for.
That's why our team builds on Retell as the primary platform for every client. I'm not saying ElevenLabs is bad. I'm saying that for production grade phone work, Retell clearly wins.

title: What Actually Goes Into a Good Voice Agent
dek: Behind the friendly voice are dozens of settings, tools, and tests. Here's what goes into a production agent on Retell AI, so you know what a solid build looks like.
videoTitle: Retell AI Basics 2026: Everything You Need to Start Building Voice Agents (New & Improved)

body.text: From the outside a voice agent looks simple. Someone calls, a friendly voice picks up, the caller gets help. Underneath that are dozens of settings, and most of what separates a good agent from one that embarrasses your business lives in details your callers never see.

I scaled my agency to $11K in a month built entirely on Retell AI, so this is what I've learned delivering for real clients. In the video I build a demo agent for a surf shop, Kai, who gives the surf report, books lessons, and helps with gear. Here's what goes into one.
It starts with the prompt

99% of the issues that come up with a voice agent come down to the prompt. It's by far the most important part. We usually build what's called a single prompt agent, and since the models keep getting smarter, it's one of the best ways to build an all around production ready agent unless you have a very specific use case.

Every prompt we write has a role, rules, steps, and skills. Agents perform best when you give them a role. And because these models are pattern matchers, we show rather than tell: we give the agent examples of exactly the output we want.

Even when a tool helps draft the prompt, we read it line by line, as tedious as that is. Otherwise something in there causes mistakes, you test and test and test, and you never knew what was in the prompt to begin with. We also keep the model's temperature at the lowest setting so the agent stays predictable, and turn on structured output when it has to call functions with precision.
Tools that let it do real work

A good agent doesn't just talk. On Retell it can end the call naturally when the caller says goodbye, do warm and cold transfers to your team (a must for production agents), hand off to another agent for a different department on the same phone system, and check availability and book appointments through a calendar integration. Custom functions connect it to your CRM or your own systems, and it can send texts.

One small detail callers notice: when the agent runs one of these tools, we have it say something like "let me check that for you." Without that setting it can literally sit silent while it's checking, and it may even get the answer back without telling the caller.

Then there's the knowledge base, your FAQs, documents, or website, which can refresh every 24 hours. We tell the agent that if the info isn't there, say it doesn't know. That prevents hallucination, so it doesn't make something up. Knowledge base formatting is honestly a skill of its own, and a well formatted one performs better.
The settings that make it sound human

This part is so important and people overlook it. A soft coffee shop or call center background sound, at around 0.80 to 0.85 volume, sounds the most natural. Interruption sensitivity usually sits in the 70s to 80s. Set it too low and a caller can be shouting while the agent keeps talking. Set it to 100 and one small word cuts it off. Backchanneling adds little "yeah"s while the caller talks. We always have background noise and background speech removal on.

There are safety settings too. A reminder like "are you still there?" about every 15 seconds, two times max. Ending the call on silence so the agent isn't sitting there burning minutes. A max call duration about 30 to 40% above the expected length, so if something goes wrong it doesn't run for two hours. And a fallback voice in case the main one fails mid call.
Testing, and getting the data out

These agents are probabilistic, not deterministic. So we regenerate an answer 10 times to see how often the agent gives the one we want, and keep fixing until it's around 9 or 10 out of 10. That way you can be sure it's consistent. We also run simulated callers, like an angry customer, against success criteria, and we can run 50 of those at the same time. Testing is probably the most important skill in this whole business.

After the call, the agent can pull out the details you care about, like the caller's name and reason for calling, and send them anywhere: an email, a Google Sheet, your CRM. And if you own the Retell account, you simply add us to your workspace.
Most of this is invisible to your callers, which is the point. If you're comparing builders, ask how they test. That answer tells you a lot.

title: How a Voice Agent Connects to the Phone System You Already Have
dek: Cloud PBX, a cell phone, or an on site system: there are only two ways to forward calls to an AI agent, and you keep your public number either way.
videoTitle: How to Connect Your Voice Agent to ANY Business Phone System (Full Guide)

body.text: One of the first questions owners ask us is some version of "will this work with our phones?" The answer is almost always yes, and you don't have to change the number on your website, Google Maps, or reviews. Your public number stays. Calls just get forwarded to the agent.
Every setup comes down to two flavors of call forwarding and one question about your phones.
Two ways to forward calls

Unconditional: every call routes straight to the agent. Your phone doesn't ring, the call passes right through your main number, and the agent answers 100% of the time. Use this when you want the AI answering every call and you want to keep your public number.

Conditional: your phone rings first, and the call only goes to the agent if a condition hits. Nobody picks up. It's after 5:00 p.m. You're already on another line. This is perfect for an after hours and overflow agent, where you still grab the calls you can and the AI acts as a safety net for the rest.
The one question: do you have a business phone system?

If yes, you're most likely on a cloud PBX like RingCentral, 8x8, or Dialpad. RingCentral is the one I tend to find most in the wild. The buttons are a little different on each, but the idea is the same. You'll have an option to forward all calls, an option to forward when there's no answer, and a place to enter the number to forward to, which is the agent's number.

In my video I set up my own RingCentral account like a real company would and walked through both. For an after hours and overflow agent, you find the rule that says "if no one answers, calls are sent to voicemail" and change it to send calls to the agent instead. Then you add an after hours rule that routes everything to the agent outside your work hours. That's it. Callers never hear "please hold while I try to connect you" followed by a voicemail box again.

If you don't have a business phone system, maybe you take calls right off your cell like a lot of roofers, HVAC techs, plumbers, and home inspectors do, we go to the carrier level. You dial a keypad code followed by the agent's number. On T-Mobile, for example, **21* followed by the agent's number forwards all calls. Other codes forward only when you don't answer, when you're busy, when your phone is off or has no signal, or all three at once. Verizon and AT&T use different codes, but it's the same idea. Most of what passes for a landline today is VOIP, and those take the same codes.
If you're a bigger company on an on site PBX, don't sweat the details. We'll just ask who manages your phones, and your IT person hops on the call.
The mistake that creates an infinite loop

Here's one I see beginners make. They set up unconditional forwarding so the agent answers 24/7, then also want the agent to transfer callers back to the owner. Think about it. If every call to your number goes straight to the agent, and the agent transfers to that same number, it just goes right back to the agent. It's transferring back to itself.

There are two clean fixes. Give the agent a separate number to transfer to, like a Google Voice or other VOIP number, and keep unconditional forwarding. Or switch to conditional forwarding, so your phone rings first and a transfer back actually reaches you instead of looping.
Why we don't port your number

Technically you could move your phone number over to the voice platform's phone provider entirely. I never recommend it. Porting a number can take days or even weeks, there's a lot of bureaucracy involved, and you end up at the mercy of that provider. Forwarding gets the same result while your number stays exactly where it is.
So whatever you're using today, there's a way to connect it. It's two flavors, one question, and a few minutes of setup once we know which one fits.

title: Why Outbound AI Calls Get Flagged as Spam Likely, and How We Prevent It
dek: You can have a great script and a clean lead list and still get zero pickups. Here's what the carriers are doing to your number and the settings that fix it.
videoTitle: Retell AI Outbound Calling: The Complete Guide

body.text: Your outbound AI agent might be getting blocked, and you'd have no idea.
Picture it. A great script, a great voice, a clean list of leads. You launch the campaign and nobody picks up. You blame the offer. It's not the offer.
What's actually happening

The phone carriers are marking your number as "spam likely." You've seen that label on your own phone. Your leads see it too, and they never answer. Sometimes the call gets blocked before it even rings.
Out of the box, most new numbers will be marked as spam. You can check yours on a site like Nomorobo or IPQualityScore. If you're already running outbound, that check is worth doing today.
The two settings most people skip

Verified phone number. This tells the carriers your number is legit, not a robocall. On Retell it means submitting a business profile, and once it's approved your number loses that spam likely label when it calls people.

Branded call. This shows your business name on the screen when you ring, instead of a random number. One catch: Verizon cuts your business name at 15 characters, while T-Mobile and AT&T give you 32. Even "Oceanside AI Solutions" gets chopped on Verizon. Keep the name short.
Retell also requires an ID verification on the account before you run batch calls, so that's part of our setup too.
Concurrency and calls per second
I wish those add ons were all it took. There's one more piece, and if you don't understand it you're likely to overspend and have your numbers blocked without knowing why.

Concurrency is how many calls happen at the same time. Retell caps you at 20 by default across all your agents, and extra slots are $8 each per month. This matters because outbound and inbound share that pool. If your outbound campaign eats all 20, the agent answering your inbound calls can get choked out, so we reserve capacity for it.

Calls per second is how fast new calls get started. Picture a swimming pool: concurrency is how much water the pool holds, and calls per second is the faucet filling it. The default is one call per second. Here's where people get burned: if you pay for 100 concurrent calls but you're starting one call per second and each call averages 30 seconds, you'll only ever have about 30 going at once. You paid for capacity you can't use.

You can raise calls per second, up to 5 on Twilio and 16 on Telnyx. Retell recommends raising it gradually, because a sudden jump can get your number blocked. That's also why Twilio is fine to start, but Telnyx is better for large scale outbound.
Lists versus live triggers

There are two ways we set up outbound calling. Batch calling is for when you have a list. You upload it with the details you want the agent to use, like each lead's first name, and schedule the campaign to run on its own, say Monday morning. The time it takes is simple math: number of leads, divided by concurrency, times the average call length. Five leads, one at a time, at 5 minutes each is 25 minutes.

API calling is for when something happens and you need to react immediately. Someone fills out a quote form, a lead moves to a new stage in your CRM, and the call fires from your own system right away. That's how speed to lead works.
Either way, we turn on voicemail detection so the agent either hangs up or leaves a short message instead of talking to a machine.
Outbound is only worth running if people pick up. So before anyone obsesses over the script, make sure your number isn't flagged.

title: Which AI Voice Should Answer Your Phones? What Held Up on Real Calls
dek: After two years testing every Retell AI voice across dozens of production agents, these are the ones that pass as human, plus the accent trick that beats all of them.
videoTitle: Retell AI Voices: The 5 Most Realistic (I Tested Every Single One)

body.text: I've tried every single voice in Retell AI across dozens of production agents over the last 2 years. Here's the catch nobody tells you: a voice that sounds great in the demo often falls apart in production. So this isn't a demo ranking. It's what held up on real calls.
If you're picking a voice for your business, this is how I'd think about it.
The top 5, from good to best
5. Chloe. Decent, not amazing. She actually sounds better on the older ElevenLabs V2 model than on V3.

4. Hayley. Smooth. And here's a trick: Retell doesn't let you drop in audio tags, but if you spell out a sound like "ahem" in the greeting, the V3 model will actually clear its throat. Tiny human touch, big jump in realism. I also set the voice speed 15 to 20% faster on her.
3. Kate. Soft and natural. I've used her on numerous production clients.
2. Ethan. The only male voice on the list, and most male voices don't hold up. If you run a truck and trailer repair shop, a mechanic shop, or other blue collar work, he really takes the cake.

1. Grace. A little controversial, and not everyone will agree. On V3 she's bubbly, and her recording has a slight room echo that reads as real instead of crisp and fake. She works great for a lot of my use cases. That said, some clients tell me they'd prefer a more laid back agent, and if that's you, Grace might not be the one.
Why the clean voices give themselves away
Some voices are so upbeat and polished nobody actually talks like that. "Hey there, I'm Paul, your dedicated helper. Let's get to work on your request." Who talks like this, honestly?
The more a voice sounds like Siri, crisp and simple English, the more callers start evaluating whether it's an AI. That's the opposite of what you want.
The accent trick

Here's the part most people miss. The voices that sound MOST human aren't the clean English ones. They're the accents. A thick accent makes the caller focus on understanding the words, not on catching the AI.

My favorites are Yumi, a Japanese accent, and Alejandro, a Spanish accent. If you're somewhere bilingual like South Texas or Miami, Alejandro can be a great option since he sounds natural in both languages. At the top it's a tie between Louie, a French accent, and Monica, an Indian accent. I've used Monica on outbound campaigns where most people had no idea they were talking to an AI.
Match the voice to the job

There's a real tradeoff. I don't make the accent voices my go to, because a lot of businesses that come to us don't want one, and a heavy accent can make it harder for the caller to understand the agent. That's not great for fast, transactional calls like booking an appointment or reading back an address. It IS great when realism is the whole point.
So we match the voice to the job and to who's calling you. A law firm, a mechanic shop, and a tech support line probably shouldn't sound the same.
And whatever voice you land on, test it on real calls, not in the demo. If you're starting from scratch, Kate or Grace is a safe place to begin.

title: Making a Voice Agent Sound Human Takes More Than a Good Voice
dek: Retell's Expressive Mode lets an agent sigh, pause, and soften its tone. The toggle is the easy part. Here's what actually makes it land on a call.
videoTitle: Retell AI Expressive Mode: Make Your Voice Agents Sound Human

body.text: You can have the most realistic voice on the platform and still sound like ChatGPT with a speaker.
That's the line I keep coming back to. Most voice agents don't have a voice problem. They have a words problem. A realistic voice reading robotic words is still a robot, and your callers can hear it.

To test this, I built a counseling agent and called it myself as someone whose dog had just died. That's about the hardest kind of call there is to get right, and it's exactly where a flat, cheerful agent falls apart.
What Expressive Mode does

Retell's Expressive Mode gives your agent audio tags: sigh, pause, clear throat, excited, gentle. 18 voices support it. You switch it on in the voice settings, and you can override Retell's default instructions for how the tags get used.
Two things to know up front. The tags are a fixed list, so the model won't reliably sneeze or cough no matter what you write. And the default instructions are a starting point. They aren't enough.
The prompt is what makes it land
Two things in the agent's own prompt do the real work.

First, an expressive delivery section with rules for your specific use case. For the counseling agent, I told it to lean on empathy, use pauses, slow down, let a feeling land, and stress the one word that matters most. A dental office or a plumbing company would get different rules.

Second, a full example conversation at the bottom of the prompt with the tags already in it. Agent, caller, agent, caller, the kind of exchange it'll actually run into. Show the model, don't just tell it.

Tag density matters too. Put a tag in every sentence and you get weird swings, excited about one thing and sighing about something sad two seconds later. Use no tags and it's flat. There's a middle, and finding it takes testing.
The settings behind it

Under the agent handbook there are three settings we lean on. The colloquial model is a tiny model trained on thousands of real phone calls that rewrites the agent's words in real time so they sound like something a person would say. It costs about 900 tokens and 50 milliseconds of latency. Then natural filler words, and high empathy.
Then voice speed. I keep mine at 1.06, because competent speakers talk 5 to 10% faster. It varies voice to voice, and you can set it to adjust to the caller.
Here's the distinction people miss. Expressive Mode controls the speech. The colloquial model controls the words. You need both.
The honest limitations

Consistency. The agent always clears its throat when told to, but the intensity varies from one run to the next. Getting a good output once doesn't mean the agent is done, so we test the same lines several times before anything ships.
Voice variance. What works on one voice won't necessarily work on another, and accents add more complexity. Switching voices means testing again.
If you're evaluating a voice agent for your business, listen past the voice itself. Ask whether it sounds like a person choosing words, or a script being read out loud. That's usually the difference.

title: Single Prompt or Conversational Flow: How Your Voice Agent Should Be Built
dek: There are two ways to build a voice agent on Retell, and one is almost always a mistake. Here's which one we use, when the other wins, and what beats both.
videoTitle: Single Prompt vs Conversational Flow in Retell AI (Which One Wins?)

body.text: There are two ways to build a voice agent: single prompt or conversational flow. After coaching 600+ builders and shipping both to production, I can tell you single prompt wins about 90% of the time.
You don't need to build one yourself to care about this. How your agent is built decides how natural it sounds, how it handles the weird questions, and how hard it is to change later.
The number one mistake
People assume conversational flow is the advanced option, so it must be better. That's the furthest thing from the truth.

When most owners picture a voice agent, they picture something that sounds human and rolls with whatever the caller says. Conversational flow is closer to the opposite. You map out every step of the call as nodes and wire them together. It's perfect for replacing a phone menu. But if you want to replace a receptionist, single prompt is the one that actually flows.
Why single prompt usually wins

It's about 1/10 the work. Picture an agent answering questions at the front desk of a barbershop. As a single prompt, we write the prompt, edit, and test. As a flow, every node has to be mapped and organized, and it gets messy fast.

It has a built in safety net. These agents run on the same kind of models as ChatGPT, trained on huge amounts of data. So when a caller asks something outside the questions you planned for, the agent can still answer naturally. A flow just hits a wall.
Fun fact: flex mode inside conversational flow is just a single prompt agent under the hood with a visual layer on top.
When conversational flow actually wins

These models are probabilistic. They pick the most likely good answer, which makes them natural, but it's also their greatest downfall. Some businesses need certain things to happen 100% of the time. If you can only get an agent to make a required transfer 84% of the time, that's not good enough.

Conversational flow gives you that hard, locked down control in exchange for some naturalness. It shines when the agent's job is to run the call, not just answer questions. Think of an agent that has to ask 30 critical medical questions where skipping even one could open the company up to a lawsuit. In that case the caller needs to understand from the start that it's a structured call.
The silver bullet that beats both

Single prompt has one real limit. Past about 8K to 12K tokens, the prompt bloats. It's like handing an employee so much information they can't juggle it. The agent costs more per answer, responds slower, and makes more mistakes.

For reference, one single prompt agent I have live for a client right now does three call transfers, updates a CRM, and answers questions from a knowledge base. That's about 5,000 tokens, and it runs well. Where single prompts break down is something like 15 tool calls or 15K tokens.

So when an agent outgrows one prompt, we build a small network of single prompt agents linked by a routing agent. Picture a simple trifecta. The router greets the caller and asks if it's an emergency. Yes goes to a locked down emergency agent. No goes to the general agent.

They share the same voice and personality, so to the caller it sounds like one system. But each agent stays small and focused, and they're isolated. The general agent can't touch the emergency lines, and the emergency agent can't touch the CRM. That clear separation is what keeps transfers from misfiring.
You get the naturalness of single prompt and the control of flow, without the bloat. That's how we build for clients: start with a single prompt, and only split it up when it grows.
